musa-pedestris-three-centuries-of-cantin:
John S. Farmer collected and annotated three centuries of canting songs and slang rhymes. The dates run from 1536 to 1896. Cant was the secret slang of beggars, thieves, and street folk. Farmer prints their ballads with notes and indexes of titles and authors.

Songs here come from Dekker, Middleton, Pierce Egan, and many unnamed singers. Titles promise beggars' curses, cadgers' balls, and costers' serenades. Some are coarse, some comic, and all are rich in lost street speech. The book saves the songs of the poor and the rogue. Scholars of slang and song still mine it for early low-life verse.
the-lives-of-the-twelve-caesars-volume-1:
Beyond the emperors, Suetonius also wrote lives of scholars, and volume thirteen of this set holds his Lives of Eminent Grammarians, in the Thomson translation revised by T. Forester. He opens by noting that grammar was far from fashionable in early Rome. A people busy with constant wars had little time for liberal arts, and the earliest learned men, Livius and Ennius, were half-Greek poets and orators who mostly translated Greek work.

Credit for bringing grammar to Rome goes to Crates of Mallos, an envoy from King Attalus. Between the second and third Punic wars he fell into an open sewer in the Palatine quarter, broke his leg, and spent his recovery giving lectures. Suetonius turns even scholarship into biography, full of accident and character.
